notes.text: I am Abraham' servant — Abraham's name, no doubt, was well known among them, and respected; and we may suppose them not altogether ignorant of his state, for Abraham knew theirs, chap. xxii, 20.

glossa.text: « I will not eat. » Because there are those who are ready to retain teachers out of temporal stipends: but they [the teachers] are unwilling to receive them [the stipends], unless they first obtain eternal things. For if they do not find fruit in souls, they scorn to take stipends for bodies; they wash not the feet, because they relieve the desires of labour with no consolation.

« And he made me swear, » etc. ((AUG. ubi supra. )) The meaning is the same, the words not all, or the same, or so spoken; which is to be said on account of those who calumniate the evangelists because in some words they do not altogether agree, although the matter and the meaning be the same; for one man wrote this book, who could have set down the things he said above, when Abraham gave the charge, or the rest, had he judged them to belong to the matter: since the truth of a narration does not require anything except that there be truth of things and of meanings, whereby the will (for the making known of which words are made) may sufficiently appear.

notes.text: Hearken — The prophet having hitherto spoken to the bridegroom, now addresseth his speech to the bride. O daughter - He speaks like an elder person, and as her spiritual father and counsellor. Incline - He uses several words, signifying the same thing, to shew his vehement desire of her good. Forget - Comparatively.
So — So thou shalt be acceptable to thy husband; which will abundantly recompence thee, for the loss of thy father's house. Thy Lord - As he is thy husband, and also as he is thy king, and God.

The daughter — The people of Tyre; as the daughter of Zion or Jerusalem, are put for their inhabitants: he mentions the Tyrians; because they among others, and before many others, were to be converted to Christ, but they are here put for all the Gentiles, whom that city fitly represents, as being the mart of the nations. A gift - To testify their homage. The rich - Of other nations.

Daughter — The spouse; so called, because she was the daughter of one king, and the wife of another. Within - In her soul. Her cloathing - She is outwardly adorned with virtuous and honourable actions.
Brought — He alludes to the custom of conducting the bride to the bride-groom's house. Companions - Her bride-maidens attending upon her.

Instead — Having directed his speech to the bride, he now returns to the bridegroom, as may be gathered both from the Hebrew words, which are of the masculine gender; and from the next verse, which unquestionably belongs unto him, and therefore this cannot be understood of Solomon, and his marriage with Pharaoh's daughter, because he had no children by her, and but very few by all his wives and concubines; and his children were so far from being made Princes in all the earth, that they enjoyed but a small part of their father's dominions, but this was fully accomplished in Christ: who instead of his fathers of the Jewish nation, had a numerous posterity of Christians of all the nations of the earth, which here and elsewhere are called princes and kings, because of their great power with God and with men.

Remembered — As he began the psalm with the celebration of the king's praises, so now he ends with it, and adds this important circumstance, that this nuptial song should not only serve for the present solemnity, but should be remembered and sung in all successive generations. The safety of the church under God's care, ver. 1-7. An exhortation to behold his works, and to trust in him, ver. 8-11. To the chief musician for the sons of Korah, A song upon Alamoth.

glossa.text: *Hear, O daughter.* ((CASS.)) The praise of the bride is lower, but fourfold: from her form, from her glory, from the maidens, from her offspring. ((AUG.)) *Hear, O daughter.* The Prophet addresses the queen, as one of the fathers. The Jews saw and slew; do thou hear the Gospel, and by believing thou shalt see God: here through an image, in time to come through sight. Or, Hear the prophecies which foretold the incarnation, and see them fulfilled.
*And the king shall desire.* ((CASS.)) Here he praises her from her form.

*Of Tyre.* ((CASS.)) By Tyre, the neighbour of Judaea, the Gentiles are designated; whence the Canaanite woman is a figure of the Church. ((CASS.)) *Of Tyre,* of the Gentiles, the whole from a part. *With gifts.* ((AUG.)) That they may offer themselves, etc., *as far as* the Gentiles, namely, who are in the straits of their sins.

*All the glory.* ((CASS.)) From the glory of the bride, as above from the power of the bridegroom. *From within.* ((AUG.)) Or inwardly. Let almsgiving therefore be in secret, where God sees. Or not in a circumcision made by hand, as in the old law, but in spiritual things. *In fringes.* ((CASS.)) The end of the garment signifies the end of the world or of man. *Golden.* Not gilded, as above, but golden, because in the end is the whole perfection, where charity is found full.

*They shall be brought to the king. ((Ibid.))* Here the bride is praised from her friends, as above from judgment. *((Ibid.)) They shall be brought,* by opportune preaching. *After her. ((Ibid.))* First unity is spoken of, afterward the enumeration of the parts is distinct, when it is said: *Virgins and her neighbours.*

*Instead of thy fathers sons are born to thee. ((Ibid.))* Or in place of the ancient fathers, worshippers of idols, the Apostles were born, princes of preaching. ((AUG.)) Or after the prophets the Apostles, after the Apostles others.

This psalm is sung on the feast of blessed Mary the Virgin, because the things which are here said generally of the Church can be referred specially to Mary. It is sung also for virgins, because it is there said: *Virgins shall be brought to the king.* And for the Apostles, because where it is said: *Sons are born to thee.* Likewise of the nativity of the Lord, because there it treats of the praise of the bridegroom and of the bride and of the nuptials of Christ and the Church, whose espousal was made in the incarnation of the Word.

notes.text: It is good — This single word implies all the three that were used before, ver. 12, "holy, just, and good."
It is no more I that can properly be said to do it, but rather sin that dwelleth in me — That makes, as it were, another person, and tyrannizes over me.
In my flesh — The flesh here signifies the whole man as he is by nature.
I find then a law — An inward constraining power, flowing from the dictate of corrupt nature.
For I delight in the law of God — This is more than "I consent to," ver. 16. The day of liberty draws near. The inward man - Called the mind, ver. 23, 25.

But I see another law in my members — Another inward constraining power of evil inclinations and bodily appetites. Warring against the law of my mind - The dictate of my mind, which delights in the law of God. And captivating me - In spite of all my resistance

Wretched man that I am — The struggle is now come to the height; and the man, finding there is no help in himself, begins almost unawares to pray, Who shall deliver me? He then seeks and looks for deliverance, till God in Christ appears to answer his question. The word which we translate deliver, implies force. And indeed without this there can be no deliverance. The body of this death - That is, this body of death; this mass of sin, leading to death eternal, and cleaving as close to me as my body to my soul. We may observe, the deliverance is not wrought yet.

I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord — That is, God will deliver me through Christ. But the apostle, as his frequent manner is, beautifully interweaves his assertion with thanksgiving; the hymn of praise answering in a manner to the voice of sorrow, "Wretched man that I am!" So then - He here sums up the whole, and concludes what he began, ver. 7. I myself - Or rather that I, the person whom I am personating, till this deliverance is wrought. Serve the law of God with my mind - My reason and conscience declare for God. But with my flesh the law of sin - But my corrupt passions and appetites still rebel. The man is now utterly weary of his bondage, and upon the brink of liberty.

glossa.text: *For that which I work.* He proves that he is a servant of sin: because what I work according to the outward man, by leaving good undone or by doing evil, I understand according to the inward man that it ought not to be worked. Truly I work what I understand not, because I both leave undone the good that I will, and do the evil that I will not. *I understand not.* Because I see that I know one thing through the law, and do another. *For not the good which I will, this I do; but what.* Being subject to sin, he does what he wills not. *I do.* I covet; not that the Apostle goes after concupiscence, and that it drags him to evils: he wrestled, he was not subjugated: he sets this forth to thee concerning himself, lest thou despair of this in thyself.

*But now.* Now redeemed: now, the grace of Christ having been received by him who before was sold under sin. *Not I.* The mind is free, the flesh captive. *It dwelleth,* although, by not consenting to it, he lives by faith. There are desires, but if they do not reign he himself does not do the thing; but he would do it if he consented. *But sin that dwelleth in me.* How does it dwell, since it is not a substance but a privation of good? Behold, the body of the first man was corrupted through sin. And that corruption, by the condition of the offence, remains in the body, holding the force of the divine sentence given in Adam, by whose fellowship the soul is stained with sin.

*For to will.* To will, not: because to will the good lies close by me, because it lies beside the flesh and rests, powerless to rise from *ab*; read *ad*, "to" the working of the good. *Close by:* because it is in a manner natural to will the good through reason, but this willing is such that it is always overcome by the force of the flesh: but the willing of God overcomes the flesh. *To will.* The things the law commands are good, so much so that he naturally loves them, and wills to do them, but the strength to accomplish is lacking.

*To will. ((AUG.))* The good man always wills not to covet at all, but he never accomplishes this in this life.

*To accomplish.* He does not say *to do*, but *to accomplish*, because he does not do nothing. He does good: because he does not consent to concupiscence; but he does not accomplish it so as not to covet at all. So also the enemy does evil, while he stirs desire, but does not accomplish it, because he does not drag him through to evil.

*For not the good which I will.* I do not find how to accomplish the good, because neither that good which I will. From the side on which it would seem the less he shows it, but on the contrary the evil, because even that which I will not, etc. Or: I do not find the good, because it is not there. For many foolish men do not find the good in a thing, which nevertheless is there.

((AUG.)) It is one thing not to covet, another not to go after one's own concupiscences. Not to covet belongs to the wholly perfect; not to go after one's own concupiscences belongs to the man fighting, to the man wrestling. Where the fight is hot, why is the victory despaired of?

*But if,* etc. He concludes the foregoing sentence: therefore I do not work it, namely the evil; from which the former question is concluded, namely that he consents to the law of God. *But sin that dwelleth in me.* Pressed by sin, he does its will, which nevertheless is by the fault of man. He says this, that he may mark from how great things God rescues man.

*I find therefore.* He had said that the law is good, that nature is good, which wills the same thing and consents to it: here he joins the good law as a helper to the good nature; and yet the outward man conquers those two joined together: so that a man, seeing that he can escape by neither, may be beholden to grace. *To him that willeth.* Only: because I cannot accomplish it, because the evil is near to reason, lying in wait in the flesh as it were at the doors of the soul, and it forces him to do another thing than the man and the law will.

*According to the inward. ((AMB.))* Because the flesh is drawn by descent from Adam it has sin in itself; if the soul were drawn by descent, sin would dwell in it also: because Adam's soul sinned. But if the soul had sin in itself, man would not know himself.

*But I see. ((AUG.))* It belongs to the body of death that the law of the members fight against the law of the mind, while the flesh lusts against the spirit. But the law of sin does not reign, when its desires are not obeyed. *The law in the members.* Rightly is the tinder of sin called a law: because it was lawfully brought about that he who did not obey his superior should not be served by his inferior, that is, the flesh. *Captive.* From the flesh, in part: because the mind fights back, and delights together in the law of God. So it is read of the Apostle himself: the mind consents not to sin, death contends, the mind consents not. There is in me something dead, something alive: what is to be hoped from thence?
*Unhappy.* Not in the mind, but in the flesh. *Who shall deliver me?* He shall be delivered when this mortal shall put on immortality, where no concupiscence shall remain.

*Therefore I myself.* Here is the third act in the law of the spirit. But because he says that he has been delivered by grace, lest anyone grow slack in his security, as though sin should hurt no further, he determines in what way the deliverance is, if he shall have remained in grace. Otherwise sin will seize him again. *I myself.* I in the flesh, I in the mind: not two, but one out of both; with the mind I consent not, with the flesh I lust.

notes.text: This generation — That is, the men of this age. They are like those froward children of whom their fellows complain, that they will be pleased no way.
John came neither eating nor drinking — In a rigorous austere way, like Elijah. And they say, He hath a devil - Is melancholy, from the influence of an evil spirit.
The Son of man came eating and drinking — Conversing in a free, familiar way. Wisdom is justified by her children - That is, my wisdom herein is acknowledged by those who are truly wise.

glossa.text: *But to whom,* etc. John being praised, he passes to rebuking those who were not moved by John's preaching: or who despise the preaching of Christ himself. John is such and so great as I have said, and so worthy that he ought to be believed: but to whom are you to be likened, who would not believe him? *He is like to children.* The children are teachers humble in spirit. Their synagogue, or Jerusalem itself, where the ordinances of God's precepts were laid up. Their equals, their fellow-tribesmen, whom they used to reproach, because they did not rise up to the praises of God with a devout heart, with the nimbleness of limbs which the dance marks. Nor by the lamentations of the prophets for the destructions already wrought or yet to be wrought were they turned to penance.

*We have piped to you.* As David: *Rejoice in God our helper, sing aloud to the God of Jacob ((Psal. LXXX))*, and the like. *We have lamented.* As: *Be converted to me with your whole heart, in fasting and in weeping and in mourning ((Joel. II))*, *and the like*

*For John came.* As then, so now also you reject both ways of salvation. We lamented to John, we piped to Christ. This is the sum. This generation neither weeps with John weeping, nor rejoices with Christ rejoicing. Nor is it a wonder if they despise the twofold way of salvation, when they spurn both fasting and the fullness that is sought; if fasting pleases, why does John displease? if fullness, why the Son of man?

*And wisdom is justified,* etc. He shows that the sons of wisdom understand that righteousness is neither in abstaining nor in eating: but in an evenness of mind in bearing want, and a temperance in not corrupting oneself through abundance. The kingdom of God is not meat and drink: of which not the use but the concupiscence is blamed, in certain books it stands: Wisdom is justified by her works, because wisdom does not seek the testimony of the voice, but of works.

echoes.text: but his delight is in Yahweh’s law. On his law he meditates day and night.
echoes.note: 'I delight in God's law after the inward man' (7:22) echoes the blessed one whose 'delight is in the law of the LORD'; Paul affirms the psalmist's delight even as he reports its frustration by the flesh.

echoes.text: I will delight myself in your statutes. I will not forget your word.
echoes.note: The psalmist's repeated delight in God's statutes ('I will delight in your statutes,' 'Oh how I love your law') stands behind 7:22's 'I delight in God's law after the inward man.'

echoes.text: For a corruptible body weighs down the soul, And the earthy frame lies heavy on a mind that is full of cares.
echoes.note: 'A perishable body weighs down the soul, and this earthy tent burdens the thoughtful mind' is the closest Second Temple parallel to Paul's body/mind conflict and 'the body of this death' (7:23-24).

echoes.text: Yahweh saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of man’s heart was continually only evil.
echoes.note: 'In my flesh dwells no good thing' (7:18) resonates with the antediluvian verdict that 'every inclination of the thoughts of the human heart was only evil continually'—the OT root of the doctrine of indwelling evil impulse.

echoes.text: Yahweh smelled the pleasant aroma. Yahweh said in his heart, “I will not again curse the ground any more for man’s sake because the imagination of man’s heart is evil from his youth; neither will I ever again strike every living thing, as I have done.
echoes.note: 'The inclination (yetser) of the human heart is evil from youth' is the scriptural seed of the rabbinic evil-impulse doctrine that frames Paul's 'sin which dwells in me' and the divided will (7:17-20).

echoes.text: Behold, I was born in iniquity. In sin my mother conceived me.
echoes.note: 'I am fleshly, sold under sin' (7:14) echoes the penitential confession of being conceived in iniquity—a self caught in sin from the inside, unable to free itself.

echoes.text: Ahab said to Elijah, “Have you found me, my enemy?” He answered, “I have found you, because you have sold yourself to do that which is evil in the sight of Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'Sold under sin' (7:14) uses the idiom of being 'sold to do evil,' as Ahab 'sold himself to do what was evil in the sight of the LORD'; the same selling-into-bondage metaphor for moral captivity.

echoes.text: How I love your law! It is my meditation all day.
echoes.note: 'Oh how I love your law! It is my meditation all the day' is the paradigmatic Torah-delight Paul invokes for the inner self that consents to the law as good (7:22, 7:16).

echoes.text: Yahweh your God will circumcise your heart, and the heart of your seed, to love Yahweh your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, that you may live.
echoes.note: The promised circumcision of the heart so as to love God is the inward-law hope behind Paul's 'inward man' delighting in God's law (7:22), even as he laments its present captivity.

echoes.text: But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says Yahweh: I will put my law in their inward parts, and in their heart will I write it; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people:
echoes.note: The new-covenant promise of the law written on the heart underlies the tension Paul dramatizes between the law of the mind/inward man and the law in the members (7:22-23)—the heart that delights versus the flesh that resists.

echoes.text: If you do well, won’t it be lifted up? If you don’t do well, sin crouches at the door. Its desire is for you, but you are to rule over it.”
echoes.note: Sin 'crouching at the door' whose desire is for Cain, which he must master, prefigures Paul's sin 'dwelling in me' and warring to bring captivity (7:17, 7:23)—personified sin contending for mastery over the self.

echoes.text: I am pained and bowed down greatly. I go mourning all day long. For my waist is filled with burning. There is no soundness in my flesh. I am faint and severely bruised. I have groaned by reason of the anguish of my heart.
echoes.note: The psalmist's groaning 'wretched' lament under the weight of his own sin parallels Paul's cry 'What a wretched man I am!' (7:24)—the OT idiom of self-directed misery awaiting deliverance.

echoes.text: Bring my soul out of prison, that I may give thanks to your name. The righteous will surround me, for you will be good to me.
echoes.note: 'Bring my soul out of prison' voices the deliverance plea that shapes Paul's 'Who will deliver me out of the body of this death?' (7:24)—captivity language answered by rescue.

echoes.text: The cords of death surrounded me, the pains of Sheol got a hold of me. I found trouble and sorrow. Then I called on Yahweh’s name: “Yahweh, I beg you, deliver my soul.”
echoes.note: 'The cords of death... the pangs of Sheol... then I called on the name of the LORD: O LORD, deliver my soul' parallels the wretched-self-to-deliverance movement of 7:24-25.

echoes.text: And I answered and said, O you earth, wherefore have you brought forth, if the mind is made out of dust, like as all other created things? For it were better that the dust itself had been unborn, so that the mind might not have been made therefrom. But now the mind grows with us, and by reason of this we are tormented, because we perish and know it. Let the race of men lament and the beasts of the field be glad; let all that are born lament, but let the […]
echoes.note: 4 Ezra's lament over the 'evil heart' (cor malignum) that burdens humanity and frustrates the good is the nearest Second Temple analogue to Paul's anatomy of the divided self enslaved by indwelling sin (7:14-24).

echoes.text: “Now therefore, my sons, listen to me, for blessed are those who keep my ways.
echoes.note: 'wisdom is justified by her children' personifies Wisdom as in Proverbs 8, where Lady Wisdom calls and her children/sons heed her; Jesus and John are vindicated as Wisdom's offspring.

echoes.text: Wisdom exalts her sons, And takes hold of those who seek her.
echoes.note: 'Wisdom exalts her sons and lays hold of those who seek her' — Second Temple Wisdom personification standing directly behind 'wisdom is justified by her children.'

echoes.text: a time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance;
echoes.note: 'a time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance' faintly underlies the children's complaint about piping/dancing and mourning/lament.

notes.text: Thy king — The Messiah. He is just - The righteous one, who cometh to fulfil all righteousness. Having salvation - To bestow on all that believe in him.

I will cut off — When the Messiah comes and sets up his kingdom, he will need no external force. Neither chariot, bow nor sword, brought salvation to him, neither shall they be mentioned in the day of his conquest. The heathen - The Heathens through him shall be reconciled unto God, and one another, Eph. ii, 17. From the river - From Euphrates to the utmost end of Canaan, to the Mediterranean sea; a type of all the world, which was in due time to be the inheritance of Christ.

As for thee — Oh Jerusalem; these words are Christ's words to her. By the blood - By my blood, in which thy covenant as confirmed; 'tis God's covenant as made by him, 'tis Zion's covenant as made for her, 'tis Christ's also as made in him. Sent forth - I have delivered the Jews out of Babylon: compared to a pit in which no water was, wherein the Jews must have perished, had not God visited them.

Turn ye — The prophet exhorts the Jews to hasten to Christ, who is the salvation and high tower of the church. Prisoners of hope - Captives, yet not without hope. Even today - In this day of lowest distress. Double - Twice as much good as thou hast suffered evil.
All — All that look up to him for help.

glossa.text: *Compassionate and merciful.* ((CAS.)) Thirdly he explains at greater length the things which in the second place he set forth briefly. As if: Deservedly in these things they shall praise, because *compassionate,* etc. The parts of praise are set down here which were set down above, but they cannot be explained one by one: for who could fully explain his works or his power? ((AUG.)) *Compassionate and merciful.* To those to whom he has given that pardon. *Patient.* To those to whom he has not yet given it, but waits that he may give it.

((CAS.)) *Tender mercies.* He begins from the works, that he may be called compassionate while he restores the fallen. *Merciful,* by nature, even while he creates. *Patient,* this he takes from the second topic of praise, namely from power, which he praises, not because he has hung the lands, restrained the seas, painted the heavens with stars, etc., but because he bears with sinners, that they may be converted. *And his tender mercies.* ((AUG.)) For if thou takest away thy evil works, and there remain in thee nothing but his works, his mercy will not let thee go: but if thou dost not let go thy own works, his severity will be upon thy works, when he shall say: *Go, ye cursed, into everlasting fire ((Matth. XXV))*.

*Let all thy works confess to thee, O Lord.* ((AUG.)) Let them praise as do those things which have not the sense of praising, which are the matter of praise: because while thou inquirest, thou findest a great power in them, which is from God.

*And thy saints.* ((CAS.)) Everything that is confesses either by itself, or through rational creatures. Or the saints, that is, angels and men. This concerning holiness: for this is the holiness of God, that the saints should owe him confession.
*The glory of the kingdom.* ((ID.)) It is taken therefore from the wonders. As if: How wonderful is he who made heaven and earth, and filled them with divers good things.
*That known.* ((ID.)) This is taken from the power of terrible things, etc., *as far as* to whom, being magnificent, nothing is compared.

*Thy kingdom,* etc. ((ID.)) He praises from the perpetuity and the effect of dominion. And this is taken from greatness: if it is great to rule for a time, it is greater to have no term of dominion.

*The Lord is faithful in all.* ((ID.)) This is taken from the abundant sweetness; whence above: *The memory of the abundance of thy sweetness. Faithful,* because his coming fulfilled the gifts. To abundance also belongs that he lifts up those who fall, raises up the crushed; whence the remembrance of sweetness is had, and is belched forth in his praises.

*Who fall down.* ((CAS.)) From their own evils, all of whom God lifts up. Or, from these temporal things, as the saints do, like Job, who lose something in the world and are made abject, and are falling: but all these he confirms, because seven times the just man falls and rises again; but the wicked are weakened in evils ((Prov. XXIV)).

*And he lifts up all that are cast down.* ((AUG.)) Those belonging to him, because he resists the proud.

notes.text: It is good — This single word implies all the three that were used before, ver. 12, "holy, just, and good."
It is no more I that can properly be said to do it, but rather sin that dwelleth in me — That makes, as it were, another person, and tyrannizes over me.
In my flesh — The flesh here signifies the whole man as he is by nature.
I find then a law — An inward constraining power, flowing from the dictate of corrupt nature.
For I delight in the law of God — This is more than "I consent to," ver. 16. The day of liberty draws near. The inward man - Called the mind, ver. 23, 25.

But I see another law in my members — Another inward constraining power of evil inclinations and bodily appetites. Warring against the law of my mind - The dictate of my mind, which delights in the law of God. And captivating me - In spite of all my resistance

Wretched man that I am — The struggle is now come to the height; and the man, finding there is no help in himself, begins almost unawares to pray, Who shall deliver me? He then seeks and looks for deliverance, till God in Christ appears to answer his question. The word which we translate deliver, implies force. And indeed without this there can be no deliverance. The body of this death - That is, this body of death; this mass of sin, leading to death eternal, and cleaving as close to me as my body to my soul. We may observe, the deliverance is not wrought yet.

I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord — That is, God will deliver me through Christ. But the apostle, as his frequent manner is, beautifully interweaves his assertion with thanksgiving; the hymn of praise answering in a manner to the voice of sorrow, "Wretched man that I am!" So then - He here sums up the whole, and concludes what he began, ver. 7. I myself - Or rather that I, the person whom I am personating, till this deliverance is wrought. Serve the law of God with my mind - My reason and conscience declare for God. But with my flesh the law of sin - But my corrupt passions and appetites still rebel. The man is now utterly weary of his bondage, and upon the brink of liberty.

glossa.text: *For that which I work.* He proves that he is a servant of sin: because what I work according to the outward man, by leaving good undone or by doing evil, I understand according to the inward man that it ought not to be worked. Truly I work what I understand not, because I both leave undone the good that I will, and do the evil that I will not. *I understand not.* Because I see that I know one thing through the law, and do another. *For not the good which I will, this I do; but what.* Being subject to sin, he does what he wills not. *I do.* I covet; not that the Apostle goes after concupiscence, and that it drags him to evils: he wrestled, he was not subjugated: he sets this forth to thee concerning himself, lest thou despair of this in thyself.

*But now.* Now redeemed: now, the grace of Christ having been received by him who before was sold under sin. *Not I.* The mind is free, the flesh captive. *It dwelleth,* although, by not consenting to it, he lives by faith. There are desires, but if they do not reign he himself does not do the thing; but he would do it if he consented. *But sin that dwelleth in me.* How does it dwell, since it is not a substance but a privation of good? Behold, the body of the first man was corrupted through sin. And that corruption, by the condition of the offence, remains in the body, holding the force of the divine sentence given in Adam, by whose fellowship the soul is stained with sin.

*For to will.* To will, not: because to will the good lies close by me, because it lies beside the flesh and rests, powerless to rise from *ab*; read *ad*, "to" the working of the good. *Close by:* because it is in a manner natural to will the good through reason, but this willing is such that it is always overcome by the force of the flesh: but the willing of God overcomes the flesh. *To will.* The things the law commands are good, so much so that he naturally loves them, and wills to do them, but the strength to accomplish is lacking.

*To will. ((AUG.))* The good man always wills not to covet at all, but he never accomplishes this in this life.

*To accomplish.* He does not say *to do*, but *to accomplish*, because he does not do nothing. He does good: because he does not consent to concupiscence; but he does not accomplish it so as not to covet at all. So also the enemy does evil, while he stirs desire, but does not accomplish it, because he does not drag him through to evil.

*For not the good which I will.* I do not find how to accomplish the good, because neither that good which I will. From the side on which it would seem the less he shows it, but on the contrary the evil, because even that which I will not, etc. Or: I do not find the good, because it is not there. For many foolish men do not find the good in a thing, which nevertheless is there.

((AUG.)) It is one thing not to covet, another not to go after one's own concupiscences. Not to covet belongs to the wholly perfect; not to go after one's own concupiscences belongs to the man fighting, to the man wrestling. Where the fight is hot, why is the victory despaired of?

*But if,* etc. He concludes the foregoing sentence: therefore I do not work it, namely the evil; from which the former question is concluded, namely that he consents to the law of God. *But sin that dwelleth in me.* Pressed by sin, he does its will, which nevertheless is by the fault of man. He says this, that he may mark from how great things God rescues man.

*I find therefore.* He had said that the law is good, that nature is good, which wills the same thing and consents to it: here he joins the good law as a helper to the good nature; and yet the outward man conquers those two joined together: so that a man, seeing that he can escape by neither, may be beholden to grace. *To him that willeth.* Only: because I cannot accomplish it, because the evil is near to reason, lying in wait in the flesh as it were at the doors of the soul, and it forces him to do another thing than the man and the law will.

*According to the inward. ((AMB.))* Because the flesh is drawn by descent from Adam it has sin in itself; if the soul were drawn by descent, sin would dwell in it also: because Adam's soul sinned. But if the soul had sin in itself, man would not know himself.

*But I see. ((AUG.))* It belongs to the body of death that the law of the members fight against the law of the mind, while the flesh lusts against the spirit. But the law of sin does not reign, when its desires are not obeyed. *The law in the members.* Rightly is the tinder of sin called a law: because it was lawfully brought about that he who did not obey his superior should not be served by his inferior, that is, the flesh. *Captive.* From the flesh, in part: because the mind fights back, and delights together in the law of God. So it is read of the Apostle himself: the mind consents not to sin, death contends, the mind consents not. There is in me something dead, something alive: what is to be hoped from thence?
*Unhappy.* Not in the mind, but in the flesh. *Who shall deliver me?* He shall be delivered when this mortal shall put on immortality, where no concupiscence shall remain.

*Therefore I myself.* Here is the third act in the law of the spirit. But because he says that he has been delivered by grace, lest anyone grow slack in his security, as though sin should hurt no further, he determines in what way the deliverance is, if he shall have remained in grace. Otherwise sin will seize him again. *I myself.* I in the flesh, I in the mind: not two, but one out of both; with the mind I consent not, with the flesh I lust.

notes.text: This generation — That is, the men of this age. They are like those froward children of whom their fellows complain, that they will be pleased no way.
John came neither eating nor drinking — In a rigorous austere way, like Elijah. And they say, He hath a devil - Is melancholy, from the influence of an evil spirit.
The Son of man came eating and drinking — Conversing in a free, familiar way. Wisdom is justified by her children - That is, my wisdom herein is acknowledged by those who are truly wise.

glossa.text: *But to whom,* etc. John being praised, he passes to rebuking those who were not moved by John's preaching: or who despise the preaching of Christ himself. John is such and so great as I have said, and so worthy that he ought to be believed: but to whom are you to be likened, who would not believe him? *He is like to children.* The children are teachers humble in spirit. Their synagogue, or Jerusalem itself, where the ordinances of God's precepts were laid up. Their equals, their fellow-tribesmen, whom they used to reproach, because they did not rise up to the praises of God with a devout heart, with the nimbleness of limbs which the dance marks. Nor by the lamentations of the prophets for the destructions already wrought or yet to be wrought were they turned to penance.

*We have piped to you.* As David: *Rejoice in God our helper, sing aloud to the God of Jacob ((Psal. LXXX))*, and the like. *We have lamented.* As: *Be converted to me with your whole heart, in fasting and in weeping and in mourning ((Joel. II))*, *and the like*

*For John came.* As then, so now also you reject both ways of salvation. We lamented to John, we piped to Christ. This is the sum. This generation neither weeps with John weeping, nor rejoices with Christ rejoicing. Nor is it a wonder if they despise the twofold way of salvation, when they spurn both fasting and the fullness that is sought; if fasting pleases, why does John displease? if fullness, why the Son of man?

*And wisdom is justified,* etc. He shows that the sons of wisdom understand that righteousness is neither in abstaining nor in eating: but in an evenness of mind in bearing want, and a temperance in not corrupting oneself through abundance. The kingdom of God is not meat and drink: of which not the use but the concupiscence is blamed, in certain books it stands: Wisdom is justified by her works, because wisdom does not seek the testimony of the voice, but of works.

echoes.text: but his delight is in Yahweh’s law. On his law he meditates day and night.
echoes.note: 'I delight in God's law after the inward man' (7:22) echoes the blessed one whose 'delight is in the law of the LORD'; Paul affirms the psalmist's delight even as he reports its frustration by the flesh.

echoes.text: I will delight myself in your statutes. I will not forget your word.
echoes.note: The psalmist's repeated delight in God's statutes ('I will delight in your statutes,' 'Oh how I love your law') stands behind 7:22's 'I delight in God's law after the inward man.'

echoes.text: For a corruptible body weighs down the soul, And the earthy frame lies heavy on a mind that is full of cares.
echoes.note: 'A perishable body weighs down the soul, and this earthy tent burdens the thoughtful mind' is the closest Second Temple parallel to Paul's body/mind conflict and 'the body of this death' (7:23-24).

echoes.text: Yahweh saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of man’s heart was continually only evil.
echoes.note: 'In my flesh dwells no good thing' (7:18) resonates with the antediluvian verdict that 'every inclination of the thoughts of the human heart was only evil continually'—the OT root of the doctrine of indwelling evil impulse.

echoes.text: Yahweh smelled the pleasant aroma. Yahweh said in his heart, “I will not again curse the ground any more for man’s sake because the imagination of man’s heart is evil from his youth; neither will I ever again strike every living thing, as I have done.
echoes.note: 'The inclination (yetser) of the human heart is evil from youth' is the scriptural seed of the rabbinic evil-impulse doctrine that frames Paul's 'sin which dwells in me' and the divided will (7:17-20).

echoes.text: Behold, I was born in iniquity. In sin my mother conceived me.
echoes.note: 'I am fleshly, sold under sin' (7:14) echoes the penitential confession of being conceived in iniquity—a self caught in sin from the inside, unable to free itself.

echoes.text: Ahab said to Elijah, “Have you found me, my enemy?” He answered, “I have found you, because you have sold yourself to do that which is evil in the sight of Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'Sold under sin' (7:14) uses the idiom of being 'sold to do evil,' as Ahab 'sold himself to do what was evil in the sight of the LORD'; the same selling-into-bondage metaphor for moral captivity.

echoes.text: How I love your law! It is my meditation all day.
echoes.note: 'Oh how I love your law! It is my meditation all the day' is the paradigmatic Torah-delight Paul invokes for the inner self that consents to the law as good (7:22, 7:16).

echoes.text: Yahweh your God will circumcise your heart, and the heart of your seed, to love Yahweh your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, that you may live.
echoes.note: The promised circumcision of the heart so as to love God is the inward-law hope behind Paul's 'inward man' delighting in God's law (7:22), even as he laments its present captivity.

echoes.text: But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says Yahweh: I will put my law in their inward parts, and in their heart will I write it; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people:
echoes.note: The new-covenant promise of the law written on the heart underlies the tension Paul dramatizes between the law of the mind/inward man and the law in the members (7:22-23)—the heart that delights versus the flesh that resists.

echoes.text: If you do well, won’t it be lifted up? If you don’t do well, sin crouches at the door. Its desire is for you, but you are to rule over it.”
echoes.note: Sin 'crouching at the door' whose desire is for Cain, which he must master, prefigures Paul's sin 'dwelling in me' and warring to bring captivity (7:17, 7:23)—personified sin contending for mastery over the self.

echoes.text: I am pained and bowed down greatly. I go mourning all day long. For my waist is filled with burning. There is no soundness in my flesh. I am faint and severely bruised. I have groaned by reason of the anguish of my heart.
echoes.note: The psalmist's groaning 'wretched' lament under the weight of his own sin parallels Paul's cry 'What a wretched man I am!' (7:24)—the OT idiom of self-directed misery awaiting deliverance.

echoes.text: Bring my soul out of prison, that I may give thanks to your name. The righteous will surround me, for you will be good to me.
echoes.note: 'Bring my soul out of prison' voices the deliverance plea that shapes Paul's 'Who will deliver me out of the body of this death?' (7:24)—captivity language answered by rescue.

echoes.text: The cords of death surrounded me, the pains of Sheol got a hold of me. I found trouble and sorrow. Then I called on Yahweh’s name: “Yahweh, I beg you, deliver my soul.”
echoes.note: 'The cords of death... the pangs of Sheol... then I called on the name of the LORD: O LORD, deliver my soul' parallels the wretched-self-to-deliverance movement of 7:24-25.

echoes.text: And I answered and said, O you earth, wherefore have you brought forth, if the mind is made out of dust, like as all other created things? For it were better that the dust itself had been unborn, so that the mind might not have been made therefrom. But now the mind grows with us, and by reason of this we are tormented, because we perish and know it. Let the race of men lament and the beasts of the field be glad; let all that are born lament, but let the […]
echoes.note: 4 Ezra's lament over the 'evil heart' (cor malignum) that burdens humanity and frustrates the good is the nearest Second Temple analogue to Paul's anatomy of the divided self enslaved by indwelling sin (7:14-24).

echoes.text: “Now therefore, my sons, listen to me, for blessed are those who keep my ways.
echoes.note: 'wisdom is justified by her children' personifies Wisdom as in Proverbs 8, where Lady Wisdom calls and her children/sons heed her; Jesus and John are vindicated as Wisdom's offspring.

echoes.text: Wisdom exalts her sons, And takes hold of those who seek her.
echoes.note: 'Wisdom exalts her sons and lays hold of those who seek her' — Second Temple Wisdom personification standing directly behind 'wisdom is justified by her children.'

echoes.text: a time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance;
echoes.note: 'a time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance' faintly underlies the children's complaint about piping/dancing and mourning/lament.

echoes.text: Wisdom has built her house. She has carved out her seven pillars.
echoes.note: Wisdom's banquet invitation supports the wider Wisdom-vindicated theme; contested as a specific source.

registers.label: Spare
lines: Come to me, says Jesus, all who are weary.
We are tired, and we have come.
Take my yoke; it is easy, and the burden is light.
We will learn the gentleness of God.
What the wise overlooked, you showed to children.
Teach us, and we will rest in you.
Come, let us worship the God who carries us.
We come for rest. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Feel the weight come off your shoulders for an hour — the yoke set down, the load you carried in laid at the door.
Come to me, and I will give you rest.
You came in tired: the week, the worry, the burdens too heavy to name out loud.
Come to me, and I will give you rest.
Jesus does not hand you a heavier load; he offers his own yoke, gentle and easy, made to fit.
Come to me, and I will give you rest.
What the clever could not grasp, God reveals to the weary and the small — so come as you are, and breathe.
Come to me, and I will give you rest. Thanks be to God!

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: You came in carrying more than you can name.
Come to me, and I will give you rest.
Set down the load; the yoke he offers is gentle.
Come to me, and I will give you rest.
What the wise missed, God shows to the weary.
Come to me, and I will give you rest.
Come, let us worship the God who carries us.
Come to me, and I will give you rest. Amen.

turn.gravity: The day sets a humble king on a donkey (Zechariah), the Lord who is gracious and slow to anger (the Psalm), and Paul gasping "I do not do the good I want" (Romans 7) — and then Jesus: "Come to me, all you who are weary." The nerve: the gospel arrives not as one more demand on the competent but as rest for the worn-out and welcome for the unimpressive.
turn.trap: "Come to me" shrinks to a self-care slogan — Jesus as a place to relax — or the yoke gets reloaded into a heavier law where real Christians just try harder. Either way the strange logic is lost: that the road to rest runs through a yoke, and the door in is to become a child.
turn.hinge: He promises rest and then hands you a yoke. A burden that is somehow light, a surrender that is somehow freedom. You cannot preach the comfort without the yoke, or the yoke without the comfort.

doors.claim: What looks like another demand is rest — the weary are not told to try harder but to trade the world's crushing yoke for a gentle one.

witnesses.author: Gregory the Great
witnesses.reading: It is a cruel yoke and a hard weight of servitude to be subject to the things of time, ambitious of earth, clinging to falling things — that is the burden Christ lifts.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: My yoke is easy — or rather gracious, sweet, benign, delightful; and my burden, contrary to those of men, is ease, liberty, and honour.

doors.say: You are carrying a yoke already; the only question is whose — come and trade it for the one that fits.
doors.do: Name one heavy thing they are dragging that Christ never asked them to carry, and have them lay it down this week.

doors.claim: The kingdom is not opened by being clever — it is hidden from the proud and shown to children, so the way in is down, not up.

witnesses.author: Augustine
witnesses.reading: The wise and understanding here are the proud; for who are the babes to whom it is revealed but the humble?

witnesses.author: Gregory the Great
witnesses.reading: He says not 'to the foolish' but 'to babes,' showing that he condemns pride, not understanding.

doors.say: You will not think your way into this; it opens to the ones small enough to receive it.
doors.do: Move the competent and capable in the room to one place they need to stop managing God and become a child again.

doors.landing: We piped and you did not dance
doors.claim: This generation rejects every tune — John's fast and Jesus' feast alike — always finding a reason to refuse God in whatever form God comes.

witnesses.author: Jerome
witnesses.reading: If fasting pleased you, why not John? If fulness, why not the Son of Man? One you called possessed, the other a glutton — no form of God would do.

witnesses.author: John Chrysostom
witnesses.reading: I and John came by opposite ways to do the same thing, like two hunters driving the same quarry from two sides — what excuse then is left?

doors.say: Notice how endlessly inventive we are at saying no to God — the austere prophet too grim, the joyful Lord too loose.
doors.do: Expose one excuse the hearer keeps ready for not answering God, and let it fall.

synthesis.convergence: Every reading sets strength against gentleness. The king comes not on a war-horse but a donkey (Zechariah); God is gracious and slow to anger (Psalm 145); Paul, worn out, cannot do the good he wills (Romans 7); and Jesus calls the weary to a yoke that is light. The day meets us at the end of our strength, not the height of it.
synthesis.claim: You do not have to be the strong one — the king is gentle, and his yoke is the one that finally carries you.
synthesis.here: For people who measure themselves by willpower and output — for whom Romans 7 is just Monday — the move is to stop white-knuckling the Christian life and come, weary, to the gentle king. Name where they are exhausted; hand them the donkey-riding Lord, not a heavier list.

turn.subtract: Three doors, three landings — rest for the weary, humility for the wise, the exposed excuse. Choose the one your people most need this week and let the other two go.
turn.source: Catena Aurea (Aquinas; J.H. Newman tr., public domain) + Wesley's Explanatory Notes, retrieved from ~/reception-corpus — attested, not authored.
